title: Behavioural interviews: stories that land
description: Fourteen lessons on preparing for behavioural rounds at product companies: how rounds are scored, building a story bank, answering the common questions, and delivery. Written for SDE2 and SWE3 candidates. All content is original and licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

items.title: What interviewers listen for
items.markdown:
## What the round is for

A coding round shows whether you can solve a problem. A behavioural round shows how you work: how you decide, how you treat people, and what happens around your code. The interviewer asks a prompt, takes notes while you talk, and later maps those notes onto a rubric. In the debrief they argue for a rating using the facts they wrote down.

That last point shapes everything in this course. Your answer is not judged on how pleasant it sounded. It is judged on the evidence it left in the interviewer's notes.

## The six things interviewers listen for

Companies name these differently, but almost every rubric covers the same ground.

- **Ownership:** Did you treat the problem as yours, even when it was not in your ticket? Did you follow it through to the end, including the dull parts?
- **Scope:** How big was the problem, in users, systems, teams and time? Scope is the size of what you were responsible for, not the size of the project you merely touched.
- **Impact:** What changed because of your work? Impact is a result someone outside your team could notice: faster pages, fewer pages at night, a launch that happened, money saved.
- **Collaboration:** How did you work with people who had different goals, skills or opinions? Did others get better results because you were there?
- **Conflict:** What did you do when you and someone else wanted different things? Interviewers want to see that you can disagree without damage and settle without winning.
- **Judgment:** When there was no clear right answer, how did you choose? Judgment shows up in the trade-offs you named, the information you gathered and the risks you accepted on purpose.

## How your words become a score

Interviewers are trained to write down actions and results, not impressions. A note such as "built a retry layer, cut failed payments from 4 percent to 0.5 percent" is strong evidence. A note such as "seemed collaborative" is weak, and a debrief tends to discard it.

Three habits make your answers easy to write down.

1. **Say "I" for what you did.** If you say "we decided" and "we shipped" for ten minutes, the interviewer cannot tell what you contributed. Use "we" for the team, then say "my part was".
2. **Give the result as a fact.** Name a number, a date or an observable change. Section 2 covers how to do this honestly.
3. **Show the reasoning at the fork.** At the moment you chose between options, say what the options were and why you picked one. This is where judgment is visible.

**Remember:** A good story with no evidence loses to an average story with clear evidence. Make your actions, decisions and results easy to quote.

## Red flags that lower a rating

These patterns tend to cost candidates, even when the story itself is fine.

- **Blame:** The manager was clueless, the teammate was lazy, the product team kept changing its mind. Even when true, a story where everyone else is the problem suggests you will be a problem too.
- **No personal action:** Every sentence starts with "we". The interviewer is left guessing.
- **A hero story:** You fixed everything alone, and nobody else appears. At SDE2 and above, working through others is part of the job.
- **No learning:** Asked about a mistake, you describe a mistake that was really a success in disguise ("I worked too hard").
- **Vague results:** "It went well" or "the client was happy" with nothing you can check.
- **Rehearsed and rigid:** A recited script that collapses at the first follow-up. Interviewers probe on purpose to see whether the story is real.
- **Inflated claims:** A number that falls apart under a simple question like "how did you measure that?"

## How to use this course

Section 2 builds your story bank. Section 3 goes through the common questions one at a time. Section 4 is about delivery and practice. Come back to this list of six signals when you choose stories: every story you prepare should show at least two of them clearly.

items.title: Levelling signals: SDE2 versus SWE3
items.markdown:
## Why level matters in a behavioural round

The same story can be a strong answer for one level and a weak one for the next. Interviewers compare what you describe with what someone at the target level is expected to do. Titles differ between companies, so this lesson uses SDE2 for a solid mid-level engineer who owns features, and SWE3 for a senior engineer who owns larger areas and shapes how others work. Judge your own stories by the work, not the title on your badge.

## The difference, side by side

```text
Dimension     | SDE2 signal                          | SWE3 signal
--------------+--------------------------------------+------------------------------------------
Scope         | A feature or service you own end     | A system, a cross-team project, or a
              | to end                               | problem that spans several services
Ambiguity     | Turns a clear goal into a plan       | Defines the goal itself, and decides
              |                                      | what not to build
Influence     | Persuades teammates and reviewers    | Persuades other teams, product and
              |                                      | sometimes leadership
Impact        | Measurable on your team's metrics    | Measurable on a business or platform
              |                                      | metric, or on how fast others ship
Mentoring     | Helps new joiners and interns        | Raises the standard of a team: reviews,
              |                                      | design docs, hiring, growing seniors
Judgment      | Weighs options you are shown         | Finds options nobody listed, and names
              |                                      | the risks of each
Failure       | Owns a mistake and fixes it          | Owns a mistake, fixes the process that
              |                                      | allowed it, and tells others
```

## What this means for your stories

**If you are aiming for SDE2:** Your stories should show that you can be trusted with a whole piece of work. Pick stories where you owned a feature from vague request to production, handled a disagreement without help from a manager, and noticed a problem nobody asked you to look at. You do not need an organisation-wide story. A well-told story about a service you owned beats an inflated one about a platform you only touched.

**If you are aiming for SWE3:** At least half your stories should show reach beyond your own tasks. Look for moments where you:

- Set the direction when the goal was unclear, rather than following one.
- Made a decision that other teams had to live with, and brought them along.
- Changed how a group works: an on-call process, a review habit, a design template.
- Grew other engineers, so the team could do more after you stepped back.
- Said no, or chose to cut scope, and explained why in terms of the business.

A story where you only executed a plan handed to you is not wrong at this level, but it does not move the rating up. Several of those in a row suggest SDE2.

**If you are between the two:** Tell stories at the higher level and be ready to be honest about its limits. Interviewers prefer a candidate who stretches and says "this part was a team decision and my contribution was X" over one who claims everything.

## Reading the question for level

Prompts often hide the level in a single word.

- "Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict" is level-neutral. A SWE3 answer shows the conflict was between teams or priorities, and that you addressed the cause as well as the symptom.
- "Tell me about a project with unclear requirements" asks an SDE2 to show initiative and a SWE3 to show how they defined the problem and aligned others on it.
- "Tell me about a time you mentored someone" asks an SDE2 for one person helped. It asks a SWE3 for a pattern, such as a person you grew into a role or a practice you started.

## Common levelling mistakes

1. **Under-selling the scale.** Candidates often say "I just fixed a slow query" when the query served a checkout path for millions of requests a day. Give the context so the interviewer can see the size.
2. **Over-selling the role.** Saying you "led" a project when you were one of four engineers. A follow-up question will expose it.
3. **Stories that are all code.** Good code stories are fine, but at SWE3 interviewers want to hear about decisions, people and trade-offs around the code.
4. **Telling every story at the same altitude.** Mix a few detailed, hands-on stories with a few that show influence.

**Remember:** Level is shown by the size of the problem you chose to handle and the number of people you moved, not by the words you use to describe yourself.

items.title: Choosing 8 to 10 stories from your work
items.markdown:
## Why a bank, not an answer per question

Interviewers have dozens of possible questions, and you cannot memorise a separate answer for each. You can prepare a small set of real stories and learn to shape them to the question. Eight to ten is enough to cover almost any loop, and few enough that you remember the details when someone asks a follow-up.

## What makes a story worth keeping

A good story passes most of these checks.

- **It happened to you.** You can describe the room, the argument, the graph. Invented or borrowed stories collapse under follow-ups.
- **You made a difference.** There is at least one decision or action that was clearly yours.
- **There was tension.** A deadline, a disagreement, a risk, a mistake or a lack of information. Stories where everything went smoothly teach the interviewer nothing.
- **The outcome is visible.** Something changed that you can name, even if the outcome was mixed.
- **It is recent enough.** Prefer the last two or three years. Older stories can work when they are your best one for a topic.
- **You are proud or at peace with it.** You can talk about it calmly, including the parts that went wrong.

## Where to find them

Do not try to remember stories in a blank room. Mine your records.

1. Go through your calendar quarter by quarter and list what you worked on.
2. Open old performance reviews, promotion write-ups and peer feedback. They list outcomes that other people credited to you.
3. Scan design documents, incident reports and post-mortems you wrote or contributed to.
4. Look at your pull requests with the longest threads. Long threads usually mean disagreement.
5. Think about on-call weeks, launches that slipped, and projects that were cancelled.

## Cover the range

Aim for a spread rather than ten variations of one theme. A useful target:

- Two stories where you drove a technical project from start to finish.
- One story about a conflict or disagreement with a peer.
- One story about disagreeing with a manager or a senior person.
- One story about a real mistake or failure.
- One story about a deadline, a trade-off or a scope cut.
- One story where you led without formal authority.
- One story where you helped someone else grow.
- One story from an unclear or changing situation.

Any single story may cover more than one of these, which lesson 4 of this section explains.

## The worksheet

Fill in one block like this for every story. Keep it short: a phrase per line is enough. The goal is to remember the facts and not to write a script.

```text
Story title      : (a name only you need, e.g. "Payment retries")
Time and team    : (year, team size, your role)
Situation        : (what was going on, in one or two lines)
The problem      : (what was at risk or broken, and for whom)
Tension          : (deadline / disagreement / unknown / mistake)
My actions       : (3 to 5 actions that were mine, in order)
Decision point   : (the fork: options considered and why I chose one)
Result           : (numbers or visible changes, with the baseline)
What others did  : (so I can credit them and separate my part)
What I learned   : (one thing I do differently now)
What I would
change           : (an honest answer, for the follow-up)
Signals shown    : (ownership / scope / impact / collaboration /
                    conflict / judgment)
Questions it fits: (list of prompts this story can answer)
```

## A filled example

```text
Story title      : Payment retries
Time and team    : 2023, team of 6, backend owner of the payments client
Situation        : Checkout calls to a third-party gateway failed during
                   its maintenance windows
The problem      : About 4 percent of payments failed on weekends, and
                   support had to refund by hand
Tension          : Product wanted a new feature that quarter, not a fix
My actions       : Measured failure causes for two weeks; proposed idempotent
                   retries with backoff; built it behind a flag; rolled
                   out to 10 percent of traffic first
Decision point   : Retry in the client vs. queue and retry later; chose the
                   client because the queue needed a new service
Result           : Failed payments from 4 percent to 0.5 percent; manual
                   refunds from about 60 a week to under 5
What I learned   : Show the cost of a problem in support hours, not just
                   in error rates, to win priority
```

## A common trap

Candidates often choose only their largest project. Large projects have many stories inside them. Split one big project into two or three separate stories (the early design argument, the launch crunch, the post-launch bug) and you will have more variety with less new material.

**Remember:** Write the worksheets down. Stories that live only in your head come out long, in the wrong order and without numbers.

items.title: The STAR and CARL structures, with a worked example
items.markdown:
## Why use a structure at all

When you are nervous, you tend to start at the beginning of the project and talk until you run out of breath. A structure keeps the story short, puts your own actions in the middle and makes sure the result is not forgotten. Pick one and stay with it.

## STAR

- **Situation:** The context in a few sentences. Where, when, how big, what was at stake.
- **Task:** What you were responsible for. This is your role, not the team's goal.
- **Action:** What you did, step by step, with the reasons for your decisions.
- **Result:** What changed, with a number or a clear observation, and what you learned.

STAR is widely known, and interviewers listen for it. Its common weakness is that Situation and Task take too long. Candidates spend two minutes on background and rush the actions.

## CARL

- **Context:** One or two sentences: team, system, stakes.
- **Action:** The core of the story. Spend about half of your time here.
- **Result:** The outcome, measured where you can.
- **Learning:** What you now do differently.

CARL merges Situation and Task and adds Learning as an explicit step. It suits failure and conflict questions, where the learning is part of what is being tested. Use whichever feels more natural; this course uses the shared idea that actions and results take the most time.

## Time budget for a 2 to 3 minute story

```text
Part                        | Share of time | Roughly
----------------------------+---------------+------------
Context (Situation + Task)  | 15 percent    | 20 seconds
Action                      | 50 percent    | 80 seconds
Result                      | 20 percent    | 30 seconds
Learning                    | 15 percent    | 20 seconds
```

## Worked example

Prompt: "Tell me about a time you improved something without being asked."

**Context.** "Last year I was one of five engineers on a notifications service. It sent about two million emails and push messages a day. After a queue migration, support started reporting that some users received the same message two or three times."

**Action.** "Nobody owned the problem, because the migration project was officially closed. I pulled a day of logs and found that duplicates only appeared when a worker restarted mid-batch: the message was sent, but the acknowledgement was lost, so the queue redelivered it. I considered two fixes. One was to shorten the acknowledgement window, which was cheap but would only reduce duplicates. The other was to store a delivery key for each message and skip repeats, which needed a small table and a code change in every sender. I chose the delivery key because duplicate emails in a billing notice cause real support cost, and a partial fix would have kept the tickets coming. I wrote a short design note, got two teammates to review it, and shipped it behind a flag, starting with the billing notices."

**Result.** "Duplicate reports fell from about 40 a week to 2 in the first month, and the two that remained were from a sender we had not moved yet. I added a section on idempotent delivery to our onboarding doc."

**Learning.** "I now ask for an idempotency story in every design review that involves a queue. The mistake was treating the migration as done when it passed the test plan, so I also started adding a two-week follow-up check to project closures."

## Why this works

- The opening sets the stakes in under 30 seconds.
- The action section says "I" and gives a reason at the fork (two options, one chosen, and why).
- The result has a before and an after, and admits that two issues remained.
- The learning is specific and changes behaviour.

The whole answer takes about two and a half minutes at a normal speaking pace.

## Mistakes to avoid when using a structure

1. **Reciting it like a form.** Do not say "the situation was". Just tell the story in that order.
2. **Skipping the decision.** If the action section is a list of tasks, there is no judgment to score. Name the alternative you did not take.
3. **Ending on the action.** "And then we shipped it" is not a result. Say what changed.

**Remember:** The structure is scaffolding. The interviewer should hear a clear story, not the names of its parts.

items.title: Quantifying impact honestly
items.markdown:
## Why numbers matter

Numbers turn a claim into evidence. "I made the build faster" is an opinion. "I cut the main build from 22 minutes to 9" is something an interviewer can write down and compare with other candidates. But a number you cannot defend is worse than no number, because the first follow-up question ("how did you measure that?") exposes it.

## What counts as a good number

You do not need revenue figures. Good numbers come from the work you actually did.

- **Speed:** Latency, build time, time to review, time to onboard, time to recover.
- **Reliability:** Error rate, incident count, pages per week, uptime.
- **Volume:** Requests per second, users affected, records processed.
- **Cost:** Infrastructure spend, support hours, manual steps removed.
- **Delivery:** Releases per week, days saved on a launch, scope delivered by a date.
- **People:** Engineers onboarded, reviews turned around, people who used your tool.

## Always give a baseline

A result without a baseline is hard to judge. Compare these.

```text
Weak                        | Strong
----------------------------+---------------------------------------------
Latency improved a lot      | p95 latency went from 1.8 s to 400 ms
Fewer on-call pages         | Night pages dropped from about 12 to 3 a week
Saved the team time         | Removed a manual step that took 2 engineers
                            | about 3 hours every release
Many users benefited        | Used by the 4 teams that deploy to the cluster
```

## When you do not have a number

Many good stories have no clean metric. Use a proxy and say that it is one.

1. **Count something nearby.** Tickets about the problem, questions in the team channel, steps in a runbook.
2. **Use a before-and-after observation.** "Before, every release needed me on a call. After, the last three went out without me."
3. **Use a range and name the source.** "Roughly 30 to 40 percent, based on the dashboard I built for this."
4. **Say what you could not measure and why.** "We had no baseline, so I compared the two weeks before and after."

Honest uncertainty is believable. Interviewers see precise numbers with no source as a warning sign.

## Honesty rules

These keep your numbers safe under questioning.

- **Use only numbers you know or can reconstruct.** If you are unsure, round and say "about".
- **Do not take the whole result.** If the team's effort produced the drop, say so, then say your share: "The drop came from three changes; mine was the caching layer, which accounted for about half."
- **Do not claim a result that came later or from something else.** If the metric moved after another team shipped a fix, say that.
- **Do not hide the cost.** If the speed-up added complexity or took two quarters, mention it. It signals judgment.
- **Do not invent a number to fill a gap.** An interviewer would rather hear "I do not remember the exact figure, it was somewhere around 15 percent" than a made-up one.

## Working out the number before the interview

For each story, spend ten minutes on this.

1. Write the baseline and the final value.
2. Write how it was measured: dashboard, load test, support queue, survey.
3. Write the time window.
4. Write what else could have caused the change.
5. Write your share, in plain words.

Then check it against records you still have, such as a dashboard, a post-mortem or an old pull request description. If your recollection and the record disagree, trust the record.

## Turning a technical number into impact

A technical metric is more persuasive when linked to a person or a cost.

- "Cut p95 latency by 300 ms" becomes "checkout felt instant, and the conversion dashboard moved by about 1 percent in the following month".
- "Reduced error rate" becomes "removed about 60 manual refunds a week for support".
- "Sped up CI by 13 minutes" becomes "for 30 engineers running CI several times a day, that is a lot of waiting we got back". If you can estimate the total time, do the arithmetic aloud.

Keep this link short and factual. One sentence is enough, and the claim should be one you can defend.

**Remember:** A modest number with a clear source beats an impressive one that you cannot explain. If you would hesitate when asked how you know, leave it out.

items.title: One story, many questions
items.markdown:
## The idea

A single strong story can answer several different prompts, if you change what you emphasise. This is what lets eight stories cover thirty questions. It also saves you from the situation where you know a perfect story but do not recognise that it fits.

## Same facts, different focus

Take the payment retries story from the previous lesson. The facts do not change. The focus does.

```text
Prompt                          | What to emphasise
--------------------------------+---------------------------------------------
Biggest technical achievement   | The design: idempotent retries, rollout in
                                | stages, how failures were measured
Taking ownership                | You noticed refunds were manual and nobody
                                | owned the cause
Handling competing priorities   | Product wanted a feature; you made the case
                                | in support hours
Using data to decide            | Two weeks of failure analysis before any
                                | code
Influencing without authority   | Persuading the product owner and the
                                | gateway team's contact
A mistake or something that     | The first version retried non-idempotent
went wrong                      | calls in one path; how you caught it
```

Each retelling uses the same events but opens with a different sentence and spends most of its time on a different part. The details you leave out matter as much as the ones you keep.

## How to retell a story for a new prompt

1. **Read the prompt for the signal.** What is being tested: conflict, ownership, judgment, failure, influence?
2. **Choose the opening line to match.** If the prompt is about conflict, start with the disagreement, not the system.
3. **Pick the two actions that best show the signal.** You do not need to list everything you did.
4. **Pick the result that fits.** A persuasion story needs the outcome of the persuasion; a technical story needs the metric.
5. **Pick the learning that fits.** A conflict story learns about communication; a technical story learns about design.

## Tag your stories

On each worksheet, write the prompts the story can answer. A simple approach is to tag by signal.

```text
Story               | Own | Scope | Impact | Collab | Conflict | Judgment
--------------------+-----+-------+--------+--------+----------+---------
Payment retries     |  X  |       |   X    |        |    X     |   X
Cutting the flaky   |  X  |   X   |   X    |   X    |          |
test suite          |     |       |        |        |          |
Reviewer standards  |     |       |        |   X    |    X     |
dispute             |     |       |        |        |          |
Missed migration    |  X  |       |        |        |          |   X
deadline            |     |       |        |        |          |
```

When you can see gaps (no stories in the "Scope" column, say), you know what to look for next.

## Do not reuse a story too often in one loop

Interviewers in a loop compare notes in the debrief. If you tell the same story three times, they will notice. Use these rules.

- **At most two uses of one story in a loop.** And only when the focus is clearly different each time.
- **Keep two or three backups.** Stories you could swap in if a prompt is a poor fit for your main set.
- **Ask which areas you have covered.** If an early interviewer has covered conflict, a later one might ask about it again. You can say "I covered a conflict story earlier. I can give a different one" and offer it.

## When a story does not fit

Do not force it. A prompt about mentoring answered with a technical story sounds like you did not listen. If none of your stories match, use a short pause: "Let me think of the best example." Ten seconds of silence is normal, and shows care. If you really have no fit, give the closest honest example and say how it differs.

## Keep the facts consistent

If you tell the same story twice in a loop, the facts must match: the same dates, numbers and team size. Write your final numbers on the worksheet and read them before every interview day. Changes between tellings look like invention.

**Remember:** Prepare stories, not scripts. A story you understand well can be reshaped on the spot, while a memorised answer can only be recited.

items.title: Conflict with a teammate and disagreeing with a manager
items.markdown:
## The prompts

- "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate."
- "Describe a conflict at work and how you handled it."
- "Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager or a more senior engineer."
- "Have you ever pushed back on a decision?"

## What the question really tests

Interviewers are not looking for a conflict you won. They are checking four things.

1. Can you disagree on substance without turning it personal?
2. Do you try to understand the other side before arguing your own?
3. Do you use evidence, not volume or seniority?
4. Can you commit to a decision you lost, and still do good work?

For the manager version, add a fifth: can you raise a concern upward without going around people or sulking afterwards?

## A strong answer outline

1. **Set the stakes in one sentence.** What was the decision and why did it matter? "We had to choose between rewriting the sync module and patching it before a launch."
2. **State both positions fairly.** Describe the other person's view in a way they would agree with. This alone separates strong answers from weak ones.
3. **Say what you did to resolve it.** For example: asked questions to learn their constraints, proposed a small experiment or prototype, wrote the trade-offs in a short document, or asked for a third opinion.
4. **Show the evidence.** A benchmark, an incident history, a customer request, a cost estimate. Evidence is what makes a disagreement useful.
5. **Give the outcome, including when you lost.** If the decision went the other way, say how you supported it. "I said I still had a concern, we agreed on a checkpoint after two weeks, and I helped with the plan."
6. **End with the relationship.** Did you still work well together? Interviewers listen for this.

For the manager version, add how you raised it: privately first, with data, and with an alternative, and what you did once the decision was made.

## Example opening lines

- "A teammate and I disagreed on whether to build our own scheduler or adopt an open-source one. I wanted the open-source one; he was worried about operating it."
- "My manager wanted to ship a feature on a date I thought was unsafe. I raised it in our one-on-one with a list of the three risks."

## Pitfalls

- **Picking a trivial disagreement.** Tabs versus spaces or a naming argument shows no judgment under stress. Pick a case with real consequences.
- **Making the other person the villain.** Even if they were wrong, describe their reasoning. Interviewers imagine working with you.
- **Winning by escalation.** "So I went to my manager and she decided in my favour" suggests that you do not resolve things yourself. If escalation was needed, explain why other steps had failed.
- **Never conceding.** A story in which you were completely right and they were completely wrong sounds implausible.
- **Giving in without a voice.** "I did not want to cause trouble, so I let it go" is the opposite problem. The point is to show you can disagree well.
- **No outcome.** End with what happened, not with "we agreed to disagree".

## Level signals

At SDE2, a good conflict is with a peer or reviewer over a design or a code change, resolved by you with evidence. At SWE3, look for conflicts between teams or priorities, where you found the real interest behind the positions and made an agreement others could keep. Also at SWE3, interviewers like to hear that you changed something so the same disagreement would not return: a design template, a decision record, a clearer ownership boundary.

## A short sample

"Our team had to decide whether to migrate to a new queue before a launch. I thought the risk was too high so close to the date. My tech lead disagreed because the old queue was already causing weekly incidents. I asked for an hour, listed what could go wrong with the migration and what could go wrong if we stayed, and found that the real worry was data loss during the switch. We agreed on a plan to dual-write for a week, with a rollback point. I had still preferred waiting until after the launch, but the plan covered my concern and I owned the rollback runbook. The migration finished two days before the launch with no lost messages."

**Remember:** The best conflict stories end with a better decision than either person started with, or with a lost argument handled well. They rarely end with someone being proven wrong.

items.title: Failure and mistakes
items.markdown:
## The prompts

- "Tell me about a time you failed."
- "Describe a mistake you made at work."
- "Tell me about a project that did not go as planned."
- "What is the biggest mistake you have made in production?"

## What the question really tests

Everyone makes mistakes. The interviewer wants to know how you behave afterwards. Specifically:

1. Do you notice and admit a problem quickly, or do you hide it?
2. Can you explain the cause clearly, without excuses?
3. What did you do to limit the damage?
4. Did you change something so it would not happen again?

A strong answer shows self-awareness, accountability and growth. The failure itself can be real and even costly, as long as it is yours and is not a disaster caused by recklessness.

## A strong answer outline

1. **Name the failure plainly.** "I deployed a migration that locked a table for eleven minutes during peak traffic." Start with the fact.
2. **Say why it happened, in your own terms.** Own the cause: "I tested it on a small copy of the data and did not check how long it would take on the real table." Do not blame the tools.
3. **Describe the response.** How you found out, who you told, and what you did in the first hour. Speed and honesty count here.
4. **Describe the fix and the follow-up.** The immediate repair, then the change to prevent a repeat: a checklist, an alert, a rule for migrations, a review step.
5. **Say what you learned and what you do differently now.** Give an example from a later project where you applied it.

## Choosing a good failure

- Pick a real mistake with real consequences, such as an outage, a missed deadline, a feature nobody used, or a misjudged estimate.
- Choose one where you can describe your own part clearly.
- Prefer one from at least a year ago, which shows you have had time to act on the lesson.
- Avoid mistakes that suggest bad faith, such as ignoring a warning or hiding an issue.

## Pitfalls

- **The disguised strength.** "My biggest failure is that I care too much" is a dodge. Interviewers recognise it immediately, and it often ends the round on a weak note.
- **A failure that was not yours.** "The vendor changed their API without notice." You can include it, but the answer must be about what you did.
- **No damage described.** If there were no consequences, it was not a failure worth the question.
- **Too much self-punishment.** A long apology is uncomfortable to listen to and does not show learning. State it, fix it, learn from it.
- **No change afterwards.** "I will be more careful" is not a change. A new alert, a new test or a new review rule is.
- **Spreading the blame.** Even in a team failure, say what you could have done differently.

## Level signals

For SDE2, a good answer owns a technical or planning error and shows the process changes you made for yourself. For SWE3, interviewers hope to hear that you also looked at the system that allowed the error: a missing safeguard, an unclear ownership boundary, a review process that did not catch it. They also like to hear that you shared the lesson with others, for example in a post-mortem or a short write-up.

## Example in brief

"Early last year I estimated a search feature at three weeks, based on a prototype that used a small dataset. I did not test with production-sized data. In week two, we found that indexing would take hours, and the feature slipped by five weeks. I told my manager the same day we found it, rewrote the estimate with a range, and brought in a teammate who had worked on indexing. We shipped a smaller version first, with a nightly index. Since then I test any estimate against production-scale data before committing, and I give ranges, not single dates. Two quarters later, that practice helped me flag a similar risk in a reporting project before it was scheduled."

**Remember:** The answer is judged by what you did after the mistake. Spend more time on the response and the change than on the mistake itself.

items.title: Tight deadlines and trade-offs
items.markdown:
## The prompts

- "Tell me about a time you had to deliver under a tight deadline."
- "Describe a time you had to make a trade-off between quality and speed."
- "Tell me about a time you had to cut scope."
- "How do you handle competing priorities?"

## What the question really tests

Product engineering is a series of trade-offs. The interviewer wants to see that you:

1. Understand what really mattered for the deadline, and what did not.
2. Make trade-offs consciously and say so, instead of rushing everything.
3. Tell stakeholders early about risk, with options.
4. Protect the things that are hard to undo: data, security, user trust.
5. Come back to clean up what you deferred.

## A strong answer outline

1. **State the constraint.** What was the deadline and why was it fixed? "A partner launch on a date we could not move."
2. **Describe the goal and the full scope.** What would "done" have looked like with unlimited time?
3. **Describe how you sorted it.** For example: must-have for launch, can follow in a week, can wait. Say who agreed with this split.
4. **Name the trade-off you made, with its cost.** "We skipped the admin screen and used a script, which meant support needed an engineer for two weeks." Interviewers trust answers that include a cost.
5. **Show communication.** When and how you raised risk to your manager and the product owner, and what options you offered.
6. **Give the result.** Did you hit the date? What was the state of quality afterwards?
7. **Say what you did about the debt.** The ticket you filed, the cleanup you scheduled, the follow-up that happened.

## Questions you can answer in the story

```text
Question the interviewer may ask  | A solid answer includes
----------------------------------+------------------------------------------
What did you decide not to do?    | A named piece of scope and why it was safe
How did you know it was safe?     | A check: a flag, a rollback, monitoring
Who did you tell and when?        | A person and a day, not "everyone"
What was the cost of the shortcut?| A concrete cost you can describe
Did you clean it up?              | A follow-up with a date or an outcome
```

## What is safe to cut and what is not

A short rule of thumb you can say aloud in an interview:

- **Usually safe to defer:** Internal tooling, polish, secondary flows, non-critical reports, extra configuration, performance work beyond what the launch needs.
- **Usually not safe to cut:** Data integrity, security checks, logging and monitoring for the new path, a rollback plan, anything that is expensive to fix after launch.

When you describe your trade-off, mention which side of this line it fell on.

## Pitfalls

- **"I worked nights and weekends."** Heroics are not a plan. Interviewers may read this as poor estimation or poor communication. If long hours were part of it, mention them briefly and focus on decisions.
- **Silent risk.** "I knew we would miss but did not want to worry anyone." Early warning is the behaviour that is tested.
- **A trade-off with no cost.** If nothing was lost, it was not a trade-off.
- **Blaming the deadline.** "Product gave an impossible date." Show what you did within the constraint.
- **Quality as an enemy.** A story that treats tests and reviews as obstacles lowers your rating, especially at SWE3.

## Level signals

At SDE2, a good answer shows you organised your own work and your part of the scope, flagged risk early and kept quality where it mattered. At SWE3, look for a story in which you negotiated scope with product, made trade-offs across several people's work, and gave leaders clear options with their consequences.

## A short sample

"Our team had five weeks to add a new payment method before a partner launch. After a day of breakdown I found the full scope was about eight weeks. I wrote a one-page plan: launch needed checkout, refunds and reconciliation; the admin dashboard and email templates could follow. I showed it to the product owner and we agreed. I raised one risk in writing, that reconciliation was done by a script and would need a person to run it daily, and we accepted that. We launched on time. The dashboard shipped three weeks later, and I replaced the script in the next sprint."

**Remember:** Say what you chose not to do. A trade-off is defined by what was left out and who agreed to it.

items.title: Leading without authority and mentoring
items.markdown:
## The prompts

- "Tell me about a time you led a project or an effort without being the manager."
- "Describe how you influenced a group to change direction."
- "Tell me about a time you mentored someone."
- "How have you helped a teammate grow?"

These two themes are linked. Both are about getting good results through other people, which is a main reason the SWE3 level exists.

## What the questions really test

For leading without authority, interviewers want to know:

1. Did you see a need and step up without being asked?
2. How did you get people to follow: by listening, by a clear plan, by earning trust, or by pressure?
3. How did you handle people who did not agree?
4. Did the group deliver, and did the others grow?

For mentoring:

1. Do you invest time in others, and do you do it well?
2. Do you adapt your help to the person, or give everyone the same advice?
3. Did the person actually improve, and can you show it?

## Leading without authority: a strong outline

1. **The gap you noticed.** "Three teams were each building their own retry logic, with different bugs."
2. **Why it was yours.** You did not wait for assignment. You were the person who felt the pain, or had the skills.
3. **How you built agreement.** Talked to each team to learn their needs, wrote a short proposal, ran a review meeting, and made it easy to say yes: a small first step, a clear owner, a trial.
4. **How you kept momentum.** Regular updates, a tracker, a demo, short checkpoints.
5. **How you handled resistance.** Name one person or team who disagreed and what you did: listened, changed the plan, or showed data.
6. **The result and what the others gained.** A shared library used by all three teams, and the one-time cost of migration shared fairly.

## Mentoring: a strong outline

1. **Who and why.** A new joiner, a junior engineer, an intern or a peer in a new area. What were they trying to do?
2. **What you noticed about them.** Their strengths and the specific gap, not a general label.
3. **What you did.** Regular one-on-ones, pairing on a real task, reviews that explained reasons, stretch work with a safety net, introductions to the right people, or tips on how to write design documents.
4. **How you adjusted.** What changed when your first approach did not work. This shows skill.
5. **What happened to them.** A concrete outcome: they led a feature, passed a hiring bar, took on-call alone, were promoted. Give it as their achievement, not yours.
6. **What you learned about helping others.** For example, asking questions instead of giving answers.

## Pitfalls

- **Confusing leading with doing.** If the story is that you did most of the work yourself, it is not a leadership story.
- **"I told them what to do."** Authority-free leadership is about persuasion. If you gave orders, the story is about something else.
- **No resistance.** Every real group effort has someone who disagrees. Leaving them out sounds invented.
- **Taking the credit.** For mentoring, say what the other person did. For leading, name the people who helped.
- **Vague mentoring.** "I helped her a lot" tells the interviewer nothing. Name an action and a result.
- **Mentoring as correction only.** A story that is only about fixing someone's mistakes sounds like a review comment.

## Level signals

SDE2 candidates should show at least one case of helping a newer engineer succeed and one case of pushing a change through peers. SWE3 candidates should show a pattern: several people grown, a practice that lasts after you leave, and influence across team boundaries. Interviewers sometimes ask "who is better because you were on the team?" It is a good prompt to have a name ready for.

## A short sample

"A new graduate joined our team and struggled with design reviews. His code was fine, but his proposals missed the risks. I did not rewrite them. I asked him to write a one-page note for his next task with three sections: options, risks, and what he would measure. I reviewed the first two with comments that were questions, such as 'what happens if the queue is down?' By the third he was finding risks himself. Six months later he led the design for a notifications feature, and I was one of several reviewers."

**Remember:** Leadership stories are judged by what the group achieved and whether others grew. Put other people in the story, and give them credit.

items.title: Ambiguous projects and your biggest technical achievement
items.markdown:
## The prompts

- "Tell me about a time you worked on a project with unclear requirements."
- "Describe a time you had to make a decision with incomplete information."
- "What is the most technically challenging thing you have built?"
- "Tell me about a project you are proud of."

## Part one: ambiguity

### What it really tests

Real work rarely arrives as a finished specification. Interviewers are checking whether you:

1. Can turn a vague request into a clear problem.
2. Ask good questions, from the right people, early.
3. Make progress when waiting for certainty would cost too much.
4. Choose reversible steps when information is missing.
5. Update your plan when new facts appear.

### A strong answer outline

1. **The ambiguity.** "Product asked for better search, with no definition of better."
2. **What you did to reduce it.** Interviewed users or support, read logs, looked at competitor behaviour, wrote down your assumptions, and asked the product owner to confirm or correct them.
3. **How you defined success.** A simple measure agreed with stakeholders: for instance, the share of searches that end with a click.
4. **How you started small.** A prototype, a flag, a pilot with a small group. Show that you chose steps that were cheap to reverse.
5. **How you handled change.** A moment when facts changed and you adjusted: "After the first pilot we learned that most failures were spelling mistakes, so we changed the plan."
6. **The result.** Measure against the success measure you defined.

### Pitfalls for ambiguity

- **Waiting for clarity.** "I asked for a specification and waited" shows the opposite of what is tested.
- **Building the whole thing on a guess.** Describe how you tested the assumptions first.
- **Complaining about product.** Treat the ambiguity as the situation, not as someone's fault.
- **No evidence for the decision.** Say what information you gathered, and how much was enough.

## Part two: your biggest technical achievement

### What it really tests

This is the one prompt where you are expected to go deep. The interviewer wants to see technical depth, ownership and judgment in the same story, and often passes the notes to an engineer who will probe the details.

### A strong answer outline

1. **The problem and why it was hard.** Not "I built a service" but "we had to serve ten thousand requests per second with a data store that could not keep up".
2. **Constraints.** Time, team size, existing systems, compatibility, budget.
3. **The options you considered.** At least two, with the main reason for rejecting each.
4. **The design you chose, in enough detail to be checked.** The data model, the key algorithm, the failure handling. Be ready for follow-ups.
5. **How you built and rolled it out.** Testing, staged rollout, monitoring.
6. **The result, with numbers.** And an honest account of trade-offs: what got harder because of your design.
7. **Your part.** Say which parts you designed, which you wrote and which others did.

### Pitfalls for technical achievements

- **Naming tools instead of problems.** "I used Kafka and Redis" says little. Say what problem each solved.
- **Too much detail too early.** Give the problem and the idea first, then go deeper if asked.
- **Exaggerating your role.** The engineer interviewer will ask what you personally wrote.
- **No trade-offs.** Every design has a downside. Naming it shows maturity.
- **Choosing something that sounds impressive but that you only half understand.** Choose the one you can defend for ten minutes.

## Level signals

For SDE2, a hard problem inside your own service is enough, as long as you can explain the design choices. For SWE3, interviewers hope for a problem with wider reach: it affected several teams, needed a decision between competing designs, or changed how others build. In both cases, say what you would do differently now. Lesson 2 of the next section shows how to answer that.

## A short sample for ambiguity

"My team was asked to make onboarding emails 'more effective'. Nobody could say what effective meant. I spent two days with support and growth, and found that the main issue was that people did not finish setting up their first project. We agreed on one measure: the share of new accounts that created a project within a week. I wrote that down, along with my assumptions, and sent it to the product owner. We tested two email variants on 10 percent of traffic. The second raised the share from 31 to 38 percent. We rolled it out and left the first variant as a fallback."

**Remember:** For ambiguity, show how you made the problem smaller. For technical achievement, show the problem, the options and the trade-off before the tools.

items.title: Timing and delivery: the 2 to 3 minute story
items.markdown:
## Why length matters

Most behavioural rounds last 45 to 60 minutes and cover three to five questions, plus time for follow-ups and your own questions. That leaves roughly ten minutes per topic. If your first answer takes six minutes, the interviewer has no room to probe, and may stop you. If it takes forty seconds, there is nothing to score. The target is two to three minutes for the first telling, then follow-ups to go deeper.

## How long is 2 to 3 minutes

At a natural speaking pace of roughly 130 to 150 words a minute, two to three minutes is about 260 to 450 words. Most people who have never timed themselves run to five or six minutes. Time yourself with a phone for each story and cut until you are inside the range.

```text
Part                | Target   | Sign you are over
--------------------+----------+------------------------------------------
Opening / context   | 20 sec   | You are explaining the system architecture
Action              | 80 sec   | You are listing every task you did
Result              | 30 sec   | You are comparing many metrics
Learning            | 20 sec   | You are repeating the story
```

## Open with a headline

Start with one sentence that tells the interviewer what the story is about and why it fits the prompt. "I will tell you about a time my manager and I disagreed about a launch date, and how we settled it." This helps the interviewer decide what to write down. It also stops you from wandering.

## Signpost as you go

Short phrases help the listener track a long answer.

- "The decision I had to make was..."
- "I considered two options..."
- "The result was..."
- "What I would take from this is..."

These also make your notes easier to quote.

## Cut what does not serve the point

When a story is too long, cut in this order.

1. Background about the system that the interviewer does not need.
2. Names of tools beyond the ones that matter to the decision.
3. Setbacks that do not change the outcome.
4. A second result. Keep the strongest.

Do not cut the decision point, your personal actions or the result.

## Voice and pace

- **Slow down on the decision.** This is the part the interviewer wants to write down.
- **Use pauses.** A one-second pause before the result lets it land.
- **Keep a plain tone.** You do not need drama. Calm and specific is more convincing.
- **Say numbers clearly.** Give the unit and the baseline: "from 22 minutes to 9".
- **Look at the camera or the person.** In remote interviews, look at the camera lens when making the main point.

## Check in, do not ramble

After about two minutes, if you still have a lot to say, finish the current point and offer: "I can go into the design or the rollout, whichever is more useful." Interviewers usually have a preference, and this gives them control.

## Remote interviews

- Have your worksheets in a second window, as short notes, not as a script. Glancing at a number is fine; reading a paragraph is obvious.
- Mute notifications.
- If there is a lag, pause between sentences so you do not talk over the interviewer.
- Keep a glass of water close. Talking for an hour dries the voice.

## Common delivery mistakes

1. **Starting with the whole history.** "So, I joined the company in 2019 and..." Begin at the problem.
2. **Reading a memorised answer.** It sounds flat, and a follow-up knocks you off track.
3. **Rushing the result.** It is the payoff of the story. Slow down for it.
4. **Filler.** A lot of "um" and "basically" is natural under stress. You can reduce it by practising aloud and by pausing instead.
5. **Apologising.** "Sorry, this is a bit long" wastes time. Just be concise.

## Practising the timing

1. Pick a story and write five bullet points: context, two key actions, result, learning.
2. Tell it aloud with a timer. Do not write it out in full.
3. Record the telling. Listen for length, filler and the missing result.
4. Cut one detail and tell it again.
5. Repeat until three tellings in a row fall between 2 and 3 minutes.

**Remember:** The first telling is an invitation to ask questions. A clear two-minute story with room to go deeper beats a complete ten-minute account.

items.title: Handling follow-ups and "what would you do differently"
items.markdown:
## Why follow-ups matter

After your first telling, the interviewer will usually ask follow-ups. These are where most of the scoring is settled. They check whether the story is real, how much you did yourself and how deeply you understand it. Treat them as an opportunity: this is where you can add the evidence you left out of the short version.

## The common types of follow-up

```text
Type              | Example                              | What is being checked
------------------+--------------------------------------+-----------------------
Your role         | What exactly did you do versus the   | Honesty about scope
                  | team?                                |
Evidence          | How did you measure that?            | Whether numbers are real
Alternatives      | Why not use the other approach?      | Judgment and depth
People            | How did the other person react?      | Collaboration
Risk              | What could have gone wrong?          | Maturity
Outcome           | What happened after launch?          | Follow-through
Reflection        | What would you do differently?       | Learning
```

## How to answer well

1. **Pause and listen to the whole question.** A short pause is a sign of thought, not weakness.
2. **Answer the question that was asked.** If you were asked about numbers, give numbers.
3. **Give the specific detail.** A name of a tool, a figure, a date, a sentence someone said. Specifics make a story credible.
4. **Admit what you do not know.** "I do not remember the exact figure. It was around 15 percent, and I can tell you where I would check." This is better than inventing.
5. **Separate your part from the team's.** "The design was agreed with two others. I wrote the retry logic and the rollout plan."
6. **Do not get defensive.** Probing is the interviewer's job. A calm answer to a pointed question reads as confidence.

## "What would you do differently?"

This is the most common reflection question and it is easy to answer badly. Two bad answers are "nothing, it went well" and a long list of regrets. A good answer is specific, honest and shows how you think.

A three-part structure works well.

1. **Name one real thing.** "I would have talked to the support team in the first week, not the third."
2. **Say why.** "It would have shown me the refund problem earlier, and we would have built the report from the start."
3. **Say what you do now.** "On my next project, I ask support for their top ten complaints before I write a design."

Keep it to about thirty seconds. One honest change is worth more than five small ones.

### Things to avoid

- **"Nothing."** It signals low self-awareness, or that you did not think about it.
- **A change that would have made the whole story unnecessary.** "I would have never taken the project" is not a useful lesson.
- **A fake weakness.** "I would have worked even harder."
- **A change that blames others.** "I would have had a better manager."
- **Too many items.** A list sounds like the project was a mess.

## When the interviewer pushes back

Sometimes an interviewer challenges a decision: "That sounds risky. Why did you not just roll back?" This is a test of how you respond to a challenge. You can:

- Acknowledge the point: "That is a fair concern."
- Explain the reasoning you had at the time, with the information you had then.
- If you now think the challenge is right, say so. "Looking back, a rollback would have been safer. I did not weigh the data risk enough."

Changing your view in front of an interviewer is a strength when it is honest.

## When you freeze

If a follow-up goes blank, buy a moment.

- "Let me think about that for a second."
- "Can I make sure I understand the question? You are asking about..."
- If still stuck, give the closest thing you do know and be clear about what you are not sure of.

## Practising follow-ups

For each story on your bank list, write five hard follow-ups you would ask if you were the interviewer. Then answer each in under a minute, aloud. A practice partner is best because they can ask follow-ups you did not predict. If you have no partner, use a recording and answer your own questions.

**Remember:** Follow-ups are not an attack on your story. They are the chance to show detail, honesty and thought. Prepare for them more than for the first telling.

items.title: Questions to ask the interviewer, and a 7-day practice plan
items.markdown:
## Why your questions matter

The end of a round usually leaves a few minutes for your questions. Interviewers notice what you ask. Good questions show that you think about how work gets done, and they help you decide if the team is a good place to work. Weak questions or none at all can leave a flat last impression.

## Questions that work

Choose two or three that fit the interviewer. Do not read a list.

### About the work

- "What is the hardest problem your team is working on right now, and what makes it hard?"
- "How does the team decide what to build next?"
- "What does a typical project look like from idea to release here?"

### About how the team works

- "How are technical disagreements usually settled on this team?"
- "What does code review look like here? How long does it usually take?"
- "How does the team handle on-call, and what has improved in the last year?"

### About growth and expectations

- "What would a strong engineer at my level have done after six months here?"
- "How do engineers here get feedback, and how often?"
- "Can you tell me about someone who grew quickly on this team, and what helped?"

### About the interviewer

- "What made you choose this team, and what has surprised you since?"
- "What is one thing you would change about how we work?"

Ask them in your own words, and listen to the answers. A follow-up to something they said shows more interest than a prepared question.

## Questions to avoid

- Anything you could find in a minute on the company website.
- Salary, leave and perks in a round with an engineer. Save these for the recruiter.
- Questions that sound like tests: "What are your weaknesses?"
- Negative questions about the interviewer's manager or the company's finances.
- "Did I do well?" It puts the interviewer in an awkward position.

## A 7-day practice plan

This plan assumes about 60 to 90 minutes a day. If your interview is sooner, combine days 1 and 2, and days 5 and 6.

1. **Day 1: Read and list.** Re-read the six signals and the level table. List every project, incident and conflict from the last three years. Aim for at least 15 candidates.
2. **Day 2: Pick and fill.** Choose 8 to 10 stories that cover the range. Fill in a worksheet for each. Write down numbers and where they come from.
3. **Day 3: Structure and time.** For each story, write five bullets in the context, action, result and learning order. Tell the first four aloud with a timer, and cut each to under three minutes.
4. **Day 4: The common questions.** Take the eight prompts in section 3. For each, choose the story that fits best and tell it aloud, shaped to that prompt. Note any prompt with no good story.
5. **Day 5: Follow-ups.** For each story, write five hard follow-ups and answer them aloud. Prepare the "what would you do differently" answer for every story.
6. **Day 6: A mock round.** Ask a friend or colleague to run a 45-minute mock: five questions, with follow-ups. If nobody is available, record yourself. Review for length, "we" versus "I", and missing results.
7. **Day 7: Light review.** Reread worksheets for numbers and facts. Prepare your questions for the interviewers. Sleep well. Do not learn new stories today.

## The day of the interview

- Reread the facts, not the scripts.
- Keep water and a notepad close.
- Between rounds, jot down which stories you used so you do not repeat them.
- After each round, spend one minute noting what worked and what you would change.

## After the loop

Whatever the result, write down the prompts you were asked and how your stories fit. This turns each loop into practice for the next. If you did not get an offer, ask the recruiter if any feedback is available. It is often brief, but sometimes it points to a clear gap.

**Remember:** Preparation is a few hours of honest work: pick real stories, write down the facts, say them aloud. Nothing here needs more cleverness than that.
